Regular walkers manage it comfortably; occasional walkers find it hard.

items.q: Why can’t you drive to Sefar?
items.a: The Tassili is a plateau reached by a climb, and the sites sit on top of it. That is precisely why the paintings are in the condition they are in, and why the days up there feel like nowhere else in Algeria.

items.q: How old is the rock art?
items.a: The paintings span roughly five to eight thousand years, recording a Sahara that was green and populated by people, herds and wild animals. Djabarren alone holds thousands of catalogued works across several distinct periods.

items.q: What languages are spoken in Algeria?
items.a: Algeria's official languages are Arabic and Tamazight (Berber). Most Algerians speak Algerian Arabic (Darija) day to day, Tamazight is widely spoken in regions like Kabylie, and French is very widely used in business, media and education. English is growing among younger people.

items.a: Algeria uses the European two-round-pin plugs, types C and F, on 230 volts at 50 Hz. Travellers from the UK, US, Australia or Japan need an adapter; most European visitors do not. US and Japanese devices may also need a voltage converter unless they are dual-voltage.

items.a: Modest, comfortable clothing. Shoulders and knees covered is the practical standard — loose trousers or long skirts with a top that covers the upper arms. A headscarf is not required except inside mosques, but carrying one is useful. Cities are more relaxed than small towns.

items.q: When is the best time to visit Algeria?
items.a: The best overall time to visit Algeria is autumn to spring — roughly October to April — when temperatures across the north and the Sahara are comfortable. The deep Sahara is best from October to March; high summer (June–August) is very hot in the south but fine on the Mediterranean coast.

items.q: Which parts of Algeria should tourists avoid?
items.a: The areas that carry warnings are the remote frontier zones with Mali, Niger and Libya, and some far-desert regions away from established routes. The northern cities, the coast, the Roman east, Kabylie and the organised Sahara circuits are not on that list. Check your own government's current advisory before you travel.

items.q: Is Algeria safe for tourists?
items.a: Yes for normal tourism in the north and on organised desert trips. Cities are generally calm and welcoming; take the usual precautions you would anywhere. The deep south and border regions are restricted and are visited only with licensed operators and permits.

items.q: Are there areas to avoid?
items.a: The border zones with Mali, Niger, Libya and parts of the far south outside authorised routes are off-limits to independent travel. Organised desert journeys keep to permitted areas with the required authorisations.

items.q: Can I travel independently?
items.a: In the north, yes, with patience and standard care. The Sahara is not for independent travel — it is organised through a licensed Algerian operator with guides, 4x4 and permits.

items.q: Do I need a visa for Algeria?
items.a: Most nationalities need a visa arranged in advance at an Algerian consulate, usually supported by an invitation/voucher from a licensed agency. Rules vary by nationality and change over time — always confirm with your consulate.

items.q: Can you help with my visa?
items.a: Yes — as a licensed Algerian operator we provide the invitation letter / tourist voucher and booking confirmation that most consulates require for a tourist visa.

items.q: Is there an e-visa or visa on arrival?
items.a: Generally not for ordinary tourism. The main exception is organised tourism to the far-south desert, where a simplified entry can be arranged for the group. Verify current rules officially before you rely on them.

items.q: When is the best time to visit Algeria?
items.a: Spring (March–May) and autumn (September–November) are best for the north — coast, Roman cities and mountains. The Sahara is a winter destination, best from November to February.

items.q: When should I visit the Sahara?
items.a: November to February, when desert temperatures are cool and clear. Summer in the deep south is dangerously hot and not suitable for travel.

items.q: Can I travel during Ramadan?
items.a: Yes — it is a special time to visit, though daytime eating options and some opening hours change. We plan itineraries around it so your trip runs smoothly.

items.q: How much does a trip to Algeria cost?
items.a: It depends on length and style. Our day tours start around €30, multi-day private tours run from a few hundred euros, and our longest, the 14-day Grand Discovery, is €1,850 per person. Each tour page lists its price.

items.q: Is Algeria expensive?
items.a: Day-to-day costs are moderate. The main cost of a trip is private guiding, transport, permits and domestic flights rather than high local prices.

items.q: What do tour prices include?
items.a: It varies by tour — each page has a "What's included / Not included" list. Typically a licensed guide, private transport and some meals or accommodation are included; international flights and visa fees are not.

items.q: How do you get around in Algeria?
items.a: Domestic flights cover the long distances (especially to the Sahara), comfortable trains link the northern cities, and private vehicles with a driver are the easiest way to tour. In the desert, travel is by 4x4 only.

items.q: Do I need to rent a car?
items.a: For the north it is possible, but most visitors prefer a private car and driver. For the south a licensed operator with a properly equipped 4x4 is required — we arrange all transport.

items.q: Are domestic flights reliable?
items.a: Air Algérie and other carriers link Algiers with the main cities and Saharan towns like Djanet and Timimoun. We advise on timings and build flights into your plan (flight cost is usually separate).

items.q: Can I use credit cards and ATMs?
items.a: Algeria is largely a cash economy. Cards are accepted only in some city hotels and rarely elsewhere, and foreign-card ATMs are unreliable. Plan to pay cash for most things.

items.q: What currency is used, and can I get it in advance?
items.a: The Algerian dinar (DZD). It cannot be obtained outside the country, so bring euros or US dollars in cash and exchange them on arrival.

items.q: How much cash should I bring?
items.a: Enough for your personal spending, meals not included in your tour, tips and souvenirs. Bring a mix of larger and smaller notes and keep them secure.

items.q: Is there wifi and mobile data?
items.a: City hotels usually have wifi. A local SIM card (Djezzy, Mobilis or Ooredoo) gives affordable data and is registered with your passport. Coverage thins out quickly in the desert.

items.q: Will my phone work in the Sahara?
items.a: In and around towns, yes. The deep desert is largely off-grid with little or no signal — part of its appeal — so let people know your plans before you head out.

items.q: What is Algerian food like?
items.a: Couscous, slow tagines, grilled meats and coastal fish, fresh bread, Saharan dates, Kabyle olive oil and mint tea poured from a height — Mediterranean and regional, and generous.

items.q: Can you cater for vegetarians or dietary needs?
items.a: Yes — vegetable couscous, salads, pulses and bread make vegetarian eating easy, and we can arrange for allergies or other needs if you tell us in advance.

items.q: Is the tap water safe to drink?
items.a: Stick to bottled water, which is cheap and widely available; it is provided on our desert trips.

items.q: Is Algeria safe for women travellers?
items.a: Generally yes, with normal precautions. Serious harassment is uncommon, but modest dress and awareness — especially outside the big cities — make for a more comfortable trip. Private, guided travel adds an extra layer of ease.

items.q: What should women wear?
items.a: Modest, loosely covering clothing is appreciated; carry a scarf for mosques and conservative areas. Beaches and big-city districts are more relaxed, especially in summer.

items.q: Do I need a permit for the Sahara?
items.a: Yes — the protected desert zones, including Tassili n'Ajjer and the Tadrart, require permits and a licensed local guide. We arrange the permits and guiding as part of any desert trip.

items.q: Can I explore the desert on my own?
items.a: No — independent deep-desert travel is restricted for safety and conservation. It is done with a licensed operator, 4x4 vehicles and the proper authorisations.

items.q: Can I take photos freely?
items.a: Landscapes, monuments and ruins are generally fine. Always ask before photographing people, and avoid photographing military and police sites and some government buildings.

items.q: Can I bring a drone?
items.a: Drones are restricted and often prohibited in Algeria. Do not bring or fly one without explicit prior authorisation — it can cause serious problems at the border or on site.

items.q: Do I need vaccinations?
items.a: No special vaccinations are required for most travellers. Make sure routine vaccinations are up to date and consult your doctor or a travel clinic, and bring any personal medication in its original packaging.

items.q: Is medical care available?
items.a: Cities have hospitals and pharmacies; the desert is remote, so carry a basic personal first-aid kit. Pharmacies are well stocked in towns.

items.q: Do I need travel insurance?
items.a: Yes — we strongly recommend comprehensive travel insurance that covers remote and desert travel. It is not included in tour prices.

items.q: What should I pack for the Sahara?
items.a: Warm layers for genuinely cold desert nights, strong sun protection, a headtorch, sturdy closed shoes, a scarf for sun and dust, and a refillable water bottle.

items.q: What about the cities and the north?
items.a: Comfortable walking shoes for the Casbah and ruins, modest clothing, and a light jacket for spring and autumn evenings. Add swimwear for the coast in summer.

items.q: How do I book a tour?
items.a: Send us your dates, group size and interests through the contact form or on WhatsApp. We check availability and any permits and confirm the details with you by email.

items.q: How and when do I pay?
items.a: Payment is arranged at booking — typically a deposit to confirm your trip and the balance before or at the start. Contact us for the current methods and terms for your tour.

items.q: Is my booking confirmed immediately?
items.a: We confirm by email or WhatsApp once we have checked availability, transport and any required permits — not automatically, so that what we confirm is real.

items.q: What is your cancellation policy?
items.a: Free cancellation up to 5 days before your tour departure date — cancel any time before then and you receive a full refund. Within 5 days of departure, costs already committed on your behalf (hotels, internal flights, guides and suppliers) may no longer be recoverable, and we refund whatever remains. Government visa fees and independently booked flights are paid to third parties and are never refundable. Full terms are confirmed in writing when you book.

items.q: Can I change my dates or itinerary?
items.a: We will do our best to accommodate changes, subject to availability and any supplier or permit conditions. Tell us as early as possible so we can adjust the plan.

Across ten days you join Algiers and Roman Tipaza, the Roman cities of Djémila and Timgad, Sétif's highlands and Constantine's bridges, and finish in the M'Zab Valley at Ghardaïa — capped by a Saharan excursion with quad biking, camel riding and sandboarding. Four UNESCO sites and the full north-to-desert sweep, with adventure and culture in equal measure. tours.w: Tadrart Rouge — 7 Days in the Red Sahara The Tadrart is the Sahara people picture before they have seen it: rose-coloured sand running up against black rock, arches the size of cathedrals, and a sky with nothing in the way. Seven days across the Tadrart Rouge: pink dunes, stone arches and prehistoric rock art, with six nights of wild bivouac. Flights and transfers included. This is the classic Djanet circuit, run at the pace the landscape deserves. Seven days, six of them ending at a bivouac you help pitch, crossing the Tadrart Rouge from Tigharghart to the great dunes of Tin Merzouga and back through the natural arches of Ajelati. tours.t: Ihrir & the Tassili — 7 Days of Oases and Ergs
tours.w: Ihrir & the Tassili — 7 Days of Oases and Ergs Everyone expects the Sahara to be dry. Ihrir is where it is not — a sunken oasis of standing water, reeds and rock pools, an hour from dunes that run to the horizon. The greener Tassili: the water-filled gueltas of Ihrir, the Essendilène canyon, Erg Admer dunes and Tikoubaouine. Flights and transfers included. If the Tadrart is the Sahara of sand, Ihrir is the Sahara of water. This circuit works the northern side of the Tassili n’Ajjer: an enclosed oasis whose gueltas hold water year-round, a canyon you can swim in when the season allows, wind-sculpted rock towers at Tikoubaouine, and the high dunes of Erg Admer for sunset. Six nights out under canvas, one in a guesthouse in Djanet on arrival, and the flight south from Algiers included in the price. tours.t: Sefar Trek — Into the Tassili Plateau on Foot
tours.w: Sefar Trek — Into the Tassili Plateau on Foot You cannot drive to Sefar. You climb to it, and you walk for days between painted walls that are five to eight thousand years old. A seven-day walking expedition onto the Tassili plateau to Sefar — the greatest open-air gallery of prehistoric painting in the Sahara. Flights included. This is the serious one. From Djanet the track climbs onto the Tassili plateau, and from there everything moves at walking pace — guides, cooks and donkey handlers carrying the camp while you cover five to seven hours a day between rock-art sites. Tin Zoumaitek and the valley of millennial cypresses, the painted 'dancers' of Tin Tazarift, the masks of Sefar Noir and the great gods of Sefar Blanc, and finally Djabarren, the largest single ensemble of paintings in the Tassili. tours.t: Algeria Grand Discovery — 14 Days, Coast to Sahara
tours.w: Algeria Grand Discovery — 14 Days, Coast to Sahara Most people choose between Roman Algeria and the Sahara. Fourteen days is what it takes to stop choosing. Two weeks, six UNESCO sites and a four-day Tadrart expedition — the Casbah, Tipaza, Djémila, Timgad and the M’Zab, on four direct domestic flights. This is the whole country in one journey, sequenced so that every internal flight is a scheduled direct service — no transits, no lost days in airports. You begin in Algiers and fly the same night to Djanet for a four-day 4×4 expedition into the Tadrart Rouge, sleeping two nights in the desert. Then the Roman east: Constantine on its gorge, Timgad, Annaba and Djémila. Back to the capital for the Casbah and the Bardo, west to Tipaza and Cherchell, and finally south again to Ghardaïa for the five fortified towns of the M’Zab and the Sebseb dunes.
